summary: The draft discovery brief provides a strong foundational analysis across segments, competitor benchmarks, and problem validation, but it contains several blocking issues that prevent approval. Specifically, it includes citations to excluded interview P06 in citation brackets, wraps unquoted marketing copy in double quotation marks (failing automated quote verification), introduces invented numbers and percentages in the experiment metrics and pricing test, omits raw and evidence-weighted counts for the dinner decision friction problem theme, and leaves two experiment headers without source citations.

objections.excerpt: The interview dataset contains 10 total interviews, of which 9 are usable and 1 is completely excluded [P01, P06, P10].
objections.problem: Interview P06 is an excluded source that must be given zero weight and never cited as a valid source tag. Citing [P06] in brackets triggers automated citation validation failures.
objections.fix: Remove [P06] from the citation bracket, citing only [P01, P10]. Discuss P06 in prose as an excluded interview due to methodological flaws without bracketed citation.

objections.excerpt: Interview P06 was given zero weight (weight 0.00) and excluded from all customer findings due to severe methodological defects, including heavily leading questions and opening responses copied verbatim from P01 [P01, P06].
objections.problem: The text places [P06] inside citation brackets. Citing excluded interviews violates ground rules and triggers validation errors.
objections.fix: Remove [P06] from the citation brackets, citing only [P01] when referencing the source of the verbatim overlap.

objections.excerpt: - Method: Launch landing pages targeting weeknight cooks testing two value propositions: "Stop buying double: shared kitchen inventory & shopping sync" versus "End the daily dinner debate: automated meal plans" [idea_brief, P02:t2, P04:t4].
objections.problem: The double quotation marks around 'Stop buying double: shared kitchen inventory & shopping sync' and 'End the daily dinner debate: automated meal plans' treat these ad copy phrases as verbatim quotes from interview transcripts. Ground rules require double quotes only for word-for-word participant quotes.
objections.fix: Remove the double quotation marks around both copy variants so they are not evaluated as transcript quotes.

objections.excerpt: - Success metric: At least 60% of households (12 of 20) submit inventory updates at least 3 times per week through day 14 without abandoning due to effort [P02:t8].
objections.problem: The figure '60%' is an invented percentage not sourced from any research finding or data snippet. Ground rules strictly prohibit inventing numbers and percentages.
objections.fix: Remove the invented percentage '60%' and specify the target strictly using the household counts (e.g., 'At least 12 of the 20 participating households submit inventory updates...').

objections.excerpt: - Success metric: Group B achieves at least a 40% higher weeknight meal completion rate and less than 15% plan abandonment compared to Group A [P05:t4].
objections.problem: The numbers '40%' and '15%' are invented figures not found in any cited source.
objections.fix: Remove the invented percentages '40%' and '15%'. Formulate the success criteria using directional comparative outcomes or explicit cohort counts.

objections.excerpt: Test subscription pricing at €3.49/month and €4.99/month behind a call-to-action requiring payment pre-authorization [C:PantryGenie, S05].
objections.problem: The price point '€3.49' is an invented number. Source S05 gives €3.50/month, C:PantryGenie gives €3.99/month, and C:SupperSync gives €4.49/month; €3.49 does not exist in any source.
objections.fix: Replace '€3.49' with a sourced price point from the competitor and benchmark data, such as '€3.50' (from S05) or '€3.99' (from C:PantryGenie).

objections.excerpt: Daily dinner decision friction exists, but its severity is mixed [P01:t2, P05:t2, S04]. Working parent P01 cited the daily mental load: "It's the mental load. Every single day somebody has to decide what's for dinner, and that somebody is me. Things disappear in the back of the fridge and I find them two weeks later, usually when they're already off." [P01:t2]. An aging 2023 study indicates adults spend 22 minutes daily deciding what to cook, although this evidence is aging [S04]. However, planning friction is contradicted in other in-target households: P09 reports zero friction after 40 years of routine, while P03 directly contradicts themselves by stating "Planning is my favourite part of the week, honestly. I would never want an app to take that away from me." [P03:t1] alongside "Deciding is exhausting. I would rather cook anything than think about what to cook." [P03:t2, P09:t1]. Under research evaluation guidelines, P03's planning friction cannot stand alone [P03:t1, P03:t2].
objections.problem: While food waste and shopping coordination provide raw interview counts and evidence-weighted support side by side, dinner decision friction omits raw interview counts and evidence-weighted calculations, violating EDA rules F05 and F10.
objections.fix: Provide raw and evidence-weighted counts side by side for the dinner decision friction theme across in-target and adjacent segments, accounting for P01, P03 (contradicted), and adjacent P05.
